touches.text: Coding Ticket: what we usually mean.
Has its own workflow stamped on it (the state string, with the cursor).
The ticket owns its refusals: a gate refuses a crossing on the ticket's behalf (ruling 2026-08-10). The gates are housed in harbor_master.
Transient: the transient tree (what the logging tree becomes).
Cairn's own sleep has a lot to do, including clearing the logging tree of things older than 30 days.

Owns the inspectors and gates (draft, moving from standalone): build_inspector, plan_inspector, ticket_inspector, corrosion, exemptions, rehearsal, determinism, import_sieve, and the tester (11; Q#33, Akien 2026-10-29). (Not diagnostic_inspector: it is base's, 17.3.) The code pipeline's inspectors and gates move to CodeMother; any that are not about code (if such existed) would not. (Q#31, Akien 2026-10-27)
TESTER MACHINE, CodeMother's (was the tester device, cairn/devices/tester/)
Runs a proof as its own process and writes a validation record (claim, caller, date, method, verdict, evidence, falsifier, horizon).
Seals: one current validation per proof, beside the proof. A seal holds while the code it measured is unchanged.
A timed-out run is its own outcome, not red (ticket 3dfceaa272ec).
Notices: what a run saw that nobody asked about, surfaced to the operator.
Test runs are transient (30 days, 4.3.2); seals are records of truth (git).
TOOLS: base, validation_store, proof_coverage, scratch, question, proof_discovery, chain, bus_client, artifact, system_word; machines ruling, build_inspector; db client
artifact: the one door a record of truth changes through, and the journal of who came through it (hash-chained, caller read from the kernel). USERS: everyone who writes a record.
gate: the == compare, in one place. A gate opens when every expected equals its actual. No oracle, ever.
The certificate is one file type you can't write. It carries a cryptographic (or similar) way to say that the right code wrote it, on this date, at this time, with these hashed findings.

A failure is not automatically "it broke, change it". After a gate refuses, an LLM checks the refusing sieve's intention and why against the ticket's why, to see which is wrong, the ticket or the sieve. The sieves stay deterministic and never weigh a why; the LLM check comes only after a failure. Its finding may pass one ticket, ideally for things like testing the sieve itself, and it must never be a lock pick (Akien, 2026-10-31). The sieve's why is the measure of its own red (Akien 2026-10-29: "why is this sieve here?"). [Q#62: What keeps the after-failure check from being a lock pick: a reader other than the builder (a cold cheap model, as rehearsal), the finding recording both whys verbatim and which lost, a pass that dies with its one ticket, a per-sieve count of passes that reds the sieve past some number? Which of these, or what else?]

A sieve's rule follows the ticket's kind (Akien, 2026-10-31: "for new/changed code tickets the rule is x, for fixit tickets the rule is y"). It is read off the ticket, so it stays deterministic, and 19.14.7 is left for what x and y do not cover.

open_questions.text: Who owns the transient tree? Draft: the Cairn device (it already owns clearing it in sleep, 5.2.1.4). And is it files on disk (as troubles are today, under ~/.cairn/logs/) or rows in the database?
Earlier (2026-08-06) sleep's trigger was idle, "3 hours without a human", not an hour of the day. Now it's a clock entry (2300). Is it the clock now, or both (at 2300, if no human for N hours)?
"Away windows" (you tell Cairn you'll be gone x to y) were ruled to the cairn device 2026-09-30. Are they entries on the same scheduled list? What does Cairn do differently while you're away?

What keeps the after-failure check from being a lock pick: a reader other than the builder (a cold cheap model, as rehearsal), the finding recording both whys verbatim and which lost, a pass that dies with its one ticket, a per-sieve count of passes that reds the sieve past some number?
